source.what: ArbiterOS's own red-team cases, replayed through its own policy kernel
source.how: arbiteros_kernel.policy_test_harness.run_policy_replay_from_spec, the offline harness. No model is called: the taint labels and policy verdicts here are computed by the kernel, not by an LLM, and reproducing this package costs nothing.
source.why_a_run: The case files carry only trace_id/prior/current. prop_trustworthiness and prop_confidentiality do not exist until the case is replayed, so a viewer built from the files alone could not draw the propagation.

how_to_read_the_counts: `refused` is the detection count — 39 of 105 — cases where some policy composed an actual refusal naming the rule and the reason. Read it with the split in `refusedByCategory`, because the suite labels every case safe or unsafe and the same refusals are a hit rate on one and a false-positive rate on the other. `intercepted` is smaller and answers a different question — not what the kernel decided but what the registry let it act on. policy_registry.json registers 11 of the 15 policies observe-only in the configuration this replay used; all of them still run on every case, and a gated policy's verdict is written to inactivate_error_type while the original response is returned unchanged. `wouldBlock` counts inactivate_error_type being non-empty — 87 of 105 — and it is NOT a detection count: 49 of those carry only the kernel's stand-in string 'policy would have modified the response', written when a gated policy reported a change without stating a reason — mostly PathBudgetPolicy. `flagged` is weaker still: any policy name recorded at all, and almost all of those are UnaryGatePolicy re-serialising a tool call's arguments, which leaves the response identical. Both are reported because omitting them would look like hiding them, and neither is a detection rate.
